penalty/add: L2 regularization adds a second term to the loss: lambda times the sum of the squared weights.
penalty/example: Say the weights are two, minus one and zero, and lambda is zero point one. Squared, they are four, one and zero.
penalty/sum: They add up to five, and lambda times five is a penalty of zero point five, added to the data loss.
penalty/lam: Lambda sets the trade. At zero the penalty vanishes; large, and keeping the weights small matters more than fitting the data.
decay/grad: The penalty's gradient is two lambda w. Each weight's slope is proportional to the weight itself.
decay/example: For two, minus one and zero, with lambda at zero point one, that is zero point four, minus zero point two, and zero.
decay/step: The gradient step adds it to the data gradient: w becomes w, minus eta times g plus two lambda w.
decay/shrink: Where the data gradient is zero, each step just multiplies the weight by one minus two eta lambda. With eta at a half, that is zero point nine: two becomes one point eight, then one point six two.
decay/pull: So every step pulls every weight a little toward zero, and only the data can pull back. That is why L2 is also called weight decay.
spread/same: Take the input one, one, one, one. The weights one, zero, zero, zero, and a quarter in every entry, both give it a score of one.
spread/pen: But their penalties differ. The first costs one squared: one. The second, four times a quarter squared: a quarter.
spread/prefer: Squaring makes big weights expensive, so L2 prefers the second: weight spread over every input, using all of the evidence a little rather than one input a lot.
